evidence.claim: The numbered highway took a different path before this designation.
evidence.quote: In the 1930s, US 611 was realigned to follow Delaware Drive between Martins Creek and Portland

evidence.claim: In the 1930s, U.S. 611 shifted from the route through Bangor to Delaware Drive between Martins Creek and Portland.
evidence.quote: In the 1930s, US 611 was realigned to follow Delaware Drive between Martins Creek and Portland, replacing the entire length of PA 827. The former alignment of the route between Martins Creek and Mount Bethel via Bangor was designated as PA 712;

evidence.claim: In 1972, Pennsylvania Route 611 replaced the U.S. designation between Philadelphia and Tobyhanna.
evidence.quote: On March 14, 1972, US 611 was decommissioned and replaced with PA 611 between Philadelphia and I-81E in Tobyhanna

evidence.claim: In Easton, the state route changed again in the 1970s, moving onto Larry Holmes Drive. Its earlier downtown course had used 3rd, Ferry, 2nd and Front streets, while the new alignment followed the riverfront.
evidence.quote: In the 1970s, PA 611 was realigned to follow Larry Holmes Drive through downtown Easton, having previously followed 3rd Street, a one-way pair along 3rd Street and Ferry Street northbound and 2nd Street southbound, Ferry Street, and Front Street.

evidence.claim: Starting in Easton, the drive follows the Delaware’s west bank into Forks Township, through woods with houses beside the river.
evidence.quote: PA 611 leaves Easton for Forks Township and runs through forested areas with some homes alongside the river, curving to the north.

evidence.claim: Beyond Sandts Eddy, Route 611 turns away from the Delaware toward Martins Creek, then crosses the creek and continues through woods into farm fields.
evidence.quote: The route enters Lower Mount Bethel Township and through Sandts Eddy.

evidence.claim: The byway continues to Riverton, where the Riverton–Belvidere Bridge connects Pennsylvania with New Jersey across the Delaware.
evidence.quote: The Riverton–Belvidere Bridge is a bridge that crosses the Delaware River and connects Belvidere, New Jersey in the east with Riverton, Pennsylvania

evidence.claim: At Easton, the Lehigh River joins the Delaware.
evidence.quote: In Easton, Pennsylvania, the Lehigh River joins the Delaware.

evidence.claim: Route 611 crosses the Lehigh on South 3rd Street, then turns onto Larry Holmes Drive along its north bank before curving beside the Delaware.
evidence.quote: The route turns northwest onto four-lane South 3rd Street and crosses the Lehigh River

evidence.claim: Route 611 crosses the Lehigh on South 3rd Street, then turns onto Larry Holmes Drive along its north bank before curving beside the Delaware.
evidence.quote: On the north bank, PA 611 turns northeast onto two-lane undivided Larry Holmes Drive, which is named for former heavyweight boxing champion Larry Holmes, and passes through commercial areas to the east of downtown Easton, running along the north bank of the Lehigh River before curving north and following the west bank of the Delaware River.

evidence.claim: The street takes its name from the former heavyweight boxing champion.
evidence.quote: Larry Holmes Drive, which is named for former heavyweight boxing champion Larry Holmes

evidence.claim: Route 611 moved onto Larry Holmes Drive in the 1970s; its previous downtown alignment used 3rd, Ferry, 2nd and Front streets.
evidence.quote: In the 1970s, PA 611 was realigned to follow Larry Holmes Drive through downtown Easton, having previously followed 3rd Street, a one-way pair along 3rd Street and Ferry Street northbound and 2nd Street southbound, Ferry Street, and Front Street.

evidence.claim: An earlier transportation link began here, too: the Delaware Division of the Pennsylvania Canal opened in 1830, running parallel to the river from Easton to Bristol.
evidence.quote: The Delaware Division of the Pennsylvania Canal, running parallel with the river from Easton to Bristol, opened in 1830.

evidence.claim: Level ground gave this area an earlier name: Flatfield, in use by the 1800s.
evidence.quote: By the 1800s, the area had developed the name of Flatfield because of its level terrain.

evidence.claim: By the Civil War it was Martinsville; Martin’s Creek came later.
evidence.quote: By the time of the Civil War, it was known as Martinsville, and later changed to Martin's Creek.

evidence.claim: James Martin arrived around 1747, operated a gristmill and later served as a colonel in the American Revolution.
evidence.quote: with James Martin arriving around 1747. Martin operated a grist mill, and later served as a colonel in the American Revolution.

evidence.claim: The Hunter-Martin Settlement Museum commemorates the area’s early history.
evidence.quote: The Hunter-Martin Settlement Museum commemorates the early history of the area.

evidence.claim: Cement manufacture later became the area’s major industry, with the Alpha Portland Cement Company closing in 1964. The creek passes the former plant before emptying into the Delaware.
evidence.quote: The major industry in the area was as the Alpha Portland Cement Company, which closed in 1964.

evidence.claim: The creek passes the former plant before emptying into the Delaware.
evidence.quote: The creek passes the former Alpha Portland Cement plant, the major industry in the town, and empties into the Delaware River.

evidence.claim: The crossing at Riverton began as a ferry before a bridge connected it with Belvidere.
evidence.quote: The board of freeholders for Warren County, New Jersey supported the replacement of the ferry with a bridge for safety of passengers.

evidence.claim: Solon Chapin, a contractor from Easton, built the first bridge in 1836.
evidence.quote: The bridge was constructed in 1836 by Solon Chapin, a contractor from Easton, Pennsylvania.

evidence.claim: Storms damaged it that year and again in 1841, but the 1903 flood destroyed it.
evidence.quote: The bridge survived two large storms in 1836 and 1841, but sustained major damage both times. In 1903, the floods that destroyed bridges along the Delaware River Valley destroyed the bridge.

evidence.claim: The replacement followed in 1904.
evidence.quote: It was rebuilt the following year, in 1904

evidence.claim: Its builders reused the wooden bridge’s three piers, raising them to clear high floodwaters.
evidence.quote: The three piers from the wooden bridge were used, and would require them to be heightened to be above any high flood waters.

evidence.claim: Tolls had ended in 1929, after the bridge commission acquired the crossing. That transfer brought extensive repairs, including new beams, new flooring and work on a pier.
evidence.quote: on June 14, 1929, the commission abolished tolls along the bridge, making it free to cross at either end. With the bridge now under the control of the toll bridge commission, extensive repairs began on the 25-year-old structure. This construction included new beams for the bridge, new flooring, and an extensive repair to one bridge pier.

evidence.claim: The crossing survived the 1955 flood with minor damage.
evidence.quote: The structure received minor damage in the flood
